newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish bonds seen dipping if rate cut too small.
newsitem.headline: Spanish bonds seen dipping if rate cut too small.

text.p: Spain's bond market could face disappointment this week if the Bank of Spain does not shave its money market rate by 50 basis points at its tender on Thursday, dealers and financial analysts said on Monday.

The market has already discounted a monetary relaxation and the 10-year futures Bono contract, which has been rising at a fast pace since August, could dip by more than a full basis point to the 105 level, they said.
The yield curve could flatten if the Bank of Spain is less generous than expected because the short end will be hit harder.

"The market has already discounted a 50 basis point cut," Juan Antonio Mielgo, economist at Bank of America in Madrid, said. "But if, as I expect, the Bank of Spain will do less than that, say 25 basis points, the market will push the yields up above eight percent for the 10-year bonds."
The Bank of Spain has lowered its official rate five times so far this year, cutting it down from nine to 7.25 percent.
The repurchase tender on October 3 will be the first one since the government approved its 1997 budget draft, which is considered to be one of the most severe Spain has ever passed.
Analysts said short dated bonds in particular could be disrupted by disappointment on the official rate.
"If the Bank of Spain doesn't the lower official rate on Thursday, the market will think it does not like the budget...this could be really dangerous," a dealer with a big Spanish bank told Reuters.
Analysts forecast that the 9.90 percent two-year note trading at a price of 105.50/53 and yielding 6.93 percent earlier on Monday could see a yield above 7.05 percent.
The 8.80 percent 10-year bond, yielding 7.93 percent earlier, could go back above 8.00 percent. It was sold just one month ago on September 3 at 8.921 percent.

Even though the central bank is likely to reward the budget draft with a 25 basis points cut, financial analysts said it could remain cautious and not trim further before September CPI data, due October 11, gives clues on the inflation trend.
"They can cut 25 points and then another 25 basis points before the year end," Mielgo said.
But this delay should not bother the market too much.

"The mood will continue to be positive in the long term," a dealer at Fimat in Madrid said. The 10-year spread over the German bunds was at 183 earlier after a low of 178 on Friday. It was over 440 basis points 12 months ago.
With a big focus on the Euro convergence, Italian and Spanish bonds saw some panic buying this month, a trend which is likely to continue until the peseta joins the single currency.
Foreign investors, who usually bet on the longest part of the curve, are likely to buy on every dip, traders said.

In a joint interview with the local financial daily Expansion and the Financial Times on Monday, Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar said Spain would do everything needed to be at the starting block of the European Monetary Union.
The December futures contract was trading at 106.39 at 1230 GMT, 43 points lower than Friday's close.
Dealers said the bonos were lower on Monday because the market was positioning itself for government bond auctions on Tuesday and Wednesday.

Earlier, the Spanish Treasury said it expected to sell some 275 billion pesetas in three and 10-year bonds, and 200 billion in five and 15-year, for a total of 475 billion, close to the 466 billion sold at the last auction in September.

"In any case I do not expect the 10-year future contract can go below 106 today or tomorrow," a dealer with Fimat said. "If we see something lower, it should be around 105.85." -- Madrid Newsroom + 341 585 2160
